newsitem.title: UK: NatWest seeks new tenants for bombed tower.
newsitem.headline: NatWest seeks new tenants for bombed tower.

text.p: A London skyscraper damaged by an IRA bomb went on the market for new tenants on Monday after a 75 million pound ($123 million) refit by its owners, Britain's National Westminster Bank.
The landmark NatWest Tower, one of London's tallest buildings and the highest in the capital's traditional financial heartland, was devastated in 1993 by an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb.

NatWest is not returning to the 183-metre-tall office building its staff evacuated after the bombing, but the bank hopes to fill the renamed International Financial Centre with a variety of tenants, although no one has signed up yet.
Lord Alexander, NatWest's chairman said the refitting of the tower marked a "remarkable transformation that has taken place almost invisibly over the last four years."
Alexander told a news briefing he would never forget the sombre moment when returned to the tower after the Bishopsgate bombing and saw the devastation caused.
He declined to say how much of the 75 million pound refurbishment cost had been borne by insurance, but said it was a highly significant proportion.
Reconstruction of the tower is due to be completed in October although David Edmonds, managing director of NatWest Group Central Services, said no tenants had yet signed up for space.
But discussions with potential occupants, whom NatWest hopes will pay an average 45 pounds per square foot, have already begun and NatWest is confident there will be considerable demand.
Tenants will be whisked to their office, a 24th floor restaurant or a 42nd floor hospitality area by what NatWest says are Europe's fastest lifts, travelling at seven metres a second.
"Its a metre a second faster than the lift in Canary Wharf," a construction engineer, still sporting a yellow hard hat, said proudly as the lift shot back down to earth after the briefing.
But Edmonds dismissed comparisons with the taller Canary Wharf tower, a few miles east along the river Thames in London's Docklands.

There has been intense rivalry between the regenerated former docks and the traditional City of London over winning the important headquarters of blue-chip financial institutions, with Docklands offering lower rents and incentive packages.

"This is a very different concept to Canary Wharf," said Edmonds. While Canary Wharf was aimed at occupiers with a need for large spaces, the International Financial Centre would be more flexible, with a mixture of tenants.

Britain's notoriously unpredictable weather means NatWest cannot always guarantee stunning views of London and the surrounding counties but it will offer tenants restaurants, private dining rooms, video-conferencing facilities and even a swimming pool.

Edmonds said NatWest would consider selling the building but not for two or three years when the tower was fully let. With a tower full of tenants, it would be worth "in excess of 200 million pounds", he told Reuters after the briefing.
Although approval for the NatWest tower design was given to well-known sixties architect Richard Seifert in 1969, it was not opened until 1980.
The building still provides the focal point for the City of London, dwarfing Sir Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral in a skyline still relatively free from skyscrapers.
